blocks.x: Now let's get back to Galadora. I would practice like mad. And during the time we were playing in the quarter, the Orphan Theatre had, for 27 years, had used the old-fashioned Pitt-type band, you know, only to play vortical. And Emil Tasso, Sr., had the job for 27 years. That's where that famous remark came from, was when he came home and told his wife, I got my notice, she said, I told you it wouldn't be a steady job. You've heard that before too. That's an epic down here. But they finally gave him his notice, and a young violinist by the name of Russo, Joseph Russo, or Joe Russo, was made the contractor, the leader actually, because in those days, they actually directed the Pitt. And he put a new type band in there. He got Howard Voorhees on trumpet and Al Galladora on saxophone, Henry Raymond on clarinet, on tenor saxophone. He had a modern type outfit. Instead of just Mr. Jufri on clarinet alone, and a flute player by the name of Jim Seger and so forth, they went into a more modern outfit. And Al got so bored playing fordable, you know, playing four shows a day, seven days a week, and you read the same music until at the end of the third show, you're not reading, you're just doing it by memory. He bought every clarinet and every saxophone. In those days, they had an F saxophone in between the E flat and the B flat. He bought an A clarinet, he bought a C clarinet, he bought a bass clarinet. And he'd go downstairs and practice each of them. And then he'd take, for instance, the A clarinet into the pit and read the B flat clarinet parts, which is a difficult transposition, half tone one way or the other, just so he could get to practice in odd keys. And as I say, when this guy, when you'd play with him, he would just sit there in astonishment, his fingers were like snakes. I've never ceased to admire this young man. But those were the days of transition because they did the same thing over at the Lowest State Theater and all these things died naturally. But these were all guys who came really from the field of dance music.
Where was Jack Asano playing? He played at the Orphan.

That's Jack. Yeah. It was the same group. I had forgotten to mention, but he and Howard were the brass team. Oh, and young Howard Reed was the second trumpet in the Orphan Theater pit. These were all young guys. I'm trying to remember who was on, I think it was Frank Cuny who played piano. And Russo on fiddle. And the bass player I think was one of the Brookhovans. I'm not too sure about that.
Did you play in a school band too?

Well, I went to Warren Easton and Mike Capera was the music teacher out there. And at that time, he didn't like me at all. I should mention that. And when I came into a certain misfortune at one time, he read it out and practically told the class, see if you guys don't behave yourselves, you'll do the same thing. Let me deviate. This is another epic story in my life. For several years after World War I, November the 11th, almost this day, was a holiday. And this particular year, the school board and its wisdom decided it would not be a holiday. And so somebody, some nut, some kid organized a strike. And at noon, he started to march around the building, gathering cohorts, you know, until finally, practically, the whole Sioux was in line. And we marched away from the school and went downtown. We took the day off. It was a holiday. We went down to the Picayune, at that time at Lafayette Square. We had our picture taken, about 300 guys. And the next day, every one of us was sentenced to 100 days after school, one hour, plus three days suspension. And that's the one that Capera, he was tickling to death that I had been hit. But now let's go back to your school band deal. Yes, we had a school band, but all we did was play in the school auditorium. We didn't go out for the football games. We had no uniforms. I don't ever remember being in a parade. And because the only guys who would study music in those days were those who later became professionals. Practically everybody in the band, most of these are dead people today, but I'm thinking of Jake Ginsberg on a trumpet, myself on saxophone, a guy by the name of Willie Rosenblum who had turned professional and long since gone. And name after name like that, but they came out of the school band, that particular school band. Was Prima in the band at that time? No. Oh no. I thought Leon, I mean Louis went to Jesuits. He went to Warren Eason. That's what I understand. It could be very possible. Because he was not in the band when I was, I was there from 23 to 26 and I went back in 27 because I wanted to take a few more courses that I needed. I was going to apply for Tulane. You know where Tulane is of course. And I wanted some more credits and I went back for half term, or what is a full term from September to January. But Louis was not in that band. Louis would have been at least two or three years younger than I am, so it's possible that he came along later on. I didn't get to meet Louis until, when would it have been, when I was with his brother Leon's band, Leon Prima and Sharko and we were rehearsing for the old Hollywood. And then Louis used to come around then and I got to know him. Because Louis' band consisted of himself, Fazzola, Johnny Viviana, and a couple of other kids his own age.
They were all, for the most part, Warren Eastern people, weren't they? I would say yes, yes, yes, yes, yes. Did you know Sterling Bowles?
I did not, no. That's a name to me. Yeah, well, one of the guys that was here, I can't remember his age. You know, there are so many people that you hear talking about.

Oh, these were all standard names. In other words, I knew about Sterling Bowles when I was just a young kid. I mean, a kid in the music business, I was 16, 17 years old, but I don't think I ever met him. As a matter of fact, to the best of my memory, he died as a fairly young man.
How old was he when he died? I don't remember. I think he died in the 1950s or 60s. Well, I didn't know him. But he left town very early, and he was making records,

I guess, while you were at Warren Eastern. I think his daughter is still a member of the local here. I don't know about that. Yes. I think her name is Mary Hugh. I'd have to look it up to be sure, but Sterling Bowles, if this is the one I'm talking about, was married to a harpist.
I don't remember. He was a big band trumpet player.

I might, yes. I'm pretty sure I'm right. I might be a little cloudy, but my name was Lavedan. She always used her maiden name. And Lucienne Lavedan, who played with the operands, she used to do some of the things with the symphony. I'm fairly certain that they had been married, and this girl would have been the daughter of that union. I think he went to Warren Easton. I think
Luke Skiro just told me about Warren Easton and different people he knew there. There's so many
of them that were there. Well, Bowles wouldn't have been younger than I. He would have been older. Get older, yeah. Sure. So I don't know how Luke could have known him. I knew Luke.
Oh, no, I'm just saying through the years I picked up the names associated with Warren Easton,

and I think Luke went there. I'm trying to, you were talking about Easton, I'm trying to remember the name of the guy who left as a young man, a trumpet player, who went to Hollywood, Los Angeles, and for years he was the standard first trumpet man on nearly all the motion picture soundtracks. He had a German name. Something like Schlegel. Wade Schlegel, sure. I remember Wade.
There could be some confusion there. Oh, sure. Well, no, there's just a million names.

Yes. Yes. Wade was in the Eastern Band too. So was Godfrey Hirsch. You see, as you're unconscious of these things come back to you. But Godfrey was a perennial student. Godfrey stayed at Warren Easton for six years, you know. I think he liked the atmosphere. And then he went to Tulane for about another 27. Yeah. And he played in the Tulaneans. Tell us about the Tulaneans. I don't know what you bought him. I didn't, I didn't work with that band. Godfrey played with that band. That was another, just a name to me. Were they a good jazz band? I would say it was fairly well liked. You know, there were no jazz bands per se with the white guys I played with. These were dance bands, right? So you'd go out with an eight-piece band or a nine-piece band. And with typical, the typical New Orleans custom, you played a few tunes. You played sets. You played from the old orchestrations, you know, the stocks. And you'd play three or four tunes. And then you'd play the waltz. And then as soon as the liquor started to work, then I didn't want to hear this anymore. Then you'd start to fake. You'd play all the standard fake tunes for the rest of the night. And I don't care whether you're talking about one of the dance halls or you're talking about at the country club. The custom followed exactly. As the evening progressed, you got into nothing but the traditional New Orleans two-beat tunes. And that's the way it was. But per se, no jazz bands. No jazz bands. No jazz bands. Every band played jazz. But you didn't have the typical combination, maybe, of, uh, we like to think about it, a piano, a banjo, and a trumpet,
a trombone, clarinet. No. What about Schofi and Leon Prima? What kind of band was that?

It was, uh, a dance band. Again, we had three saxes, three brass, and four rhythm. Uh, this was in the day of the open air dance hall. The first one that I remember was the old Frolics on St. Anne Street, just a few feet away from Broad, North Broad. And that's where I played with, uh, Skiro. He had that job out there. The butcher I mentioned. Joe Skiro. And then, uh, I...
Joe Skiro? I'm confused. The guy from, uh, Dauphine and Iberville?
I'm pretty sure, yes. He had. Clancy, you said before. Clancy, I'm sorry. I said Skiro. We've been to Skiro. That's senile at the cause of these things. Forgive it.
Well, I hate to do that to you. I'm glad you did. I'm leading you. But I didn't want you to

contradict this. No. Well, I usually do anyhow. Okay. But, uh, I played out there, yes. And then, uh, uh, Leon and, uh, Schalker had both worked out there, but not together. They had each worked out there, I should say. And they had decided to go into business, so Hip Kinley, who had run a successful 25 cents club... No, I've got this backwards now. He opened the 25 club later? Let me think about that for a moment. But anyhow, the three of them invested enough money that they took over the Hollywood, and I don't know whether it was reconstructed or what, another big open air pavilion. And they organized the band for that. And the saxophone section was myself, Fazzola, Nina Piconi, uh, Leon Prima, Schalky, and, uh, Julian Lane with the brass section. Augie Chalang was on drums, Louis Macinta was on bass, Frank Pinero was on piano, and, uh, what else do I need? Louis Macinta. Louis Macinta. Fredo Louis Macinta played guitar. That was, that was the size of the band. And I wrote some arrangements for them, sketches more than anything else, uh, to use on the fake tunes, because we did have a full band. But, uh, it was a dance band. You'd play a reading tune, then you might play a fake tune, then once in a while you'd play a waltz, you'd play sets, and there'd be a wrestler if these kids changed partners, and they did a phenomenal business down there.
Yeah. Did the, did the black bands also think of themselves as dance orchestras?

I can't answer that with any accuracy, but the, the, there were some dance bands, because I can think of some of the big bands that played, uh, for instance, out of Spanish Fort. This was what, about a 10 to 11, 12 piece band. And then some of the bands that played at the, uh, New Orleans Country Club, but they did precisely the same things. That, they'd play music, popular music, and then they'd play a couple of jazz tunes. So the, the custom was actually a New Orleans custom, rather than a band custom, or let's say a white band custom, or anything else. This was, uh, the more reason of the day, you know, that people wanted it this way. Who played lead at the Hollywood? In which band? At the Hollywood, with, uh, Premon. Oh, Leon, Leon, because Leon, uh,
read music a lot better than Sharky. Could Sharky play second parts by ear?

Oh no, he, Sharky could read, but he, he was, he was a rehearsal reader, if you know what I mean. He'd have to rehearse a tune a few times to get it. But then, when, when we played the jazz tunes, Sharky would, uh, would run the brass section, you see.
They have many side readers in the band?
Well, I think Leon would have been a side reader. Panera was a side reader.
Really?
Oh. Frank, oh, Frank played fine. He was the one that later went with Louis.
Yeah. Yeah.

Uh, Fred Lloyd Cantor read pretty good on guitar. In the sax section, we were all side readers. Uh-huh. When did you start writing? I don't know. I always liked it. And, uh, I, I could never play piano, but I would use a piano just to, to sound chords. I still can't play. I can just make a chord if I studied my fingers long enough. But, uh, I would say, within five years from the time I started, I just liked it. It was a creative thing that I liked, you know, that you could write something and make people play it. Which band did you write the most for? Oh, the Dawn Busters. Dawn Busters? Oh, for years I, with the acceptance of stocks, I wrote practically everything that they had. And, uh, well, that, that's another long, almost dull story where the Dawn Busters came from. Well, Boris. Boring band. No, it wasn't a boring band. It wasn't, far from being a boring band. It was, it was the results of guys who liked to play music. And the driving spirit, I must say, was Ray Benitez. Yeah. Because Ray Benitez organized what was nothing but a rehearsal band. We used to do it mostly in the studios at WSMB, way up on the 13th floor of the Maison Blanche building, with no idea of getting a job. And I wrote some orchestrations, Johnny Ronigan wrote some, and we'd rehearse like mad. And at that time, I was living on charters near St. Rock and Nina, Johnny Ronigan, and myself would get together and just play saxophone things. I'd write some, Johnny would write some, we'd make a little look at a stock, just try to blend and all. You know, none of us ever got tired. We'd play it six hours at home and go play a four hour job. This was fine. And the genesis of that was that Ray was trying to promote the job at what was then the Beverly Gardens, or suburban gardens, I'm sorry, later it was the Beverly Gardens. And he finally succeeded, but they told him we'd need somebody to counter front the band, because they were, it was a gambling house and they wanted to, you know, an actual guy to stay in the front of the band. And Ray decided on Pinky Vidakovich. He had a lot of personality, he had a lot of friends. And so Pinky at that time was playing in Memphis, we were rehearsing in WSMP. And finally the, the job in Memphis collapsed and Pinky came home. And so all he had to do was go out with Ray to, to talk to the owners of the place. And we got the job out there as this band. We lasted out there about six weeks. And then the club collapsed. I don't know whether we helped it to collapse or what. But this became the nucleus for the Dawn Busters, this exact same band. When WWL decided that they wanted a staff band, they hired us to go in there. And the, the only difference is that we added a violin, because I don't know why exactly, but the violin became a part of the band. But this is where the Dawn Busters came from. We were the WWL staff at that time. And then years later when they decided that they wanted to try to change, change something different, the Dawn Busters went on as a morning feature. But we were on the air at WWL, I guess about, oh, three or four or five years. I don't even remember how long off the top of my head. As a staff band, we played three times a day at 10.30, 12.30, and 5.30. 30-minute programs. And on Sunday we did a concert.
We're talking about the early and mid-30s now, are we?
I would say about 19, 20. Yes, you're right. Yes, it would have been 32, something like that.
Well, how long did the Dawn Busters last then?

The Dawn Busters itself would have been, I think, I'm trusting memory for a minute, somewhere around 41, 42. They stopped in 41 or 42? No, we started. We started. We started. We went off the air as Dawn Busters in 59. And then I left the station in 60. And then I left the station in 60. But I was with the station altogether for 27 years. But the Dawn Busters, as the Dawn Busters, this was the same band really.
Oh, who was the violinist that you had?
Carl Marder. M-A-U-D-E-R-E-R.
Thank God we got somebody to spell. These names are really hard, like Lelke. And you know, I can't figure out how to spell. Marcel German, how was it German?
Oh, he was a cellist. G-U-E-R-M-A-N-N. G-U-E-R. G-U-E-R. He was Flemish, I think. Either Flemish or pure Belgian, whatever it is. He was a nut.
In the 30s, you also went off to New York, right?

I? No. No, no, no. I didn't go to New York then at all. Did you? I went to Jackson, Mississippi in 1929 and spent practically a year up there with Harry Barth, who had a little road band there, very unsuccessful. This was a starvation trip. We had a lot of fun. Harry Barth had played bass with Ted Lewis for years, and he was a Mississippi boy, wanted to come home and start his own band, and it didn't work out, you know. When did you first go to New York? Oh, I didn't get to New York. I've never been to New York as a musician. I've been to New York as a visitor. I went up there a couple of times when I was working on staff at WWL, because they used to take care of the library, physically take care of the library, and we were a CBS affiliate, which they still are, and I'd get up there to try to do things. But I've never played in New York. That's
been a great regret. You had something to do with the recording sessions that Sharkey did in New York

in the late 30s. Oh! Yes, I did. And Benny Pollack got this date for Sharkey, and Sharkey called me long distance, and in those days that was quite a thing when you got a long distance call, you know, that he needed some material. That he had, not a contract, but he had an agreement he'd make so many sides, I think for Decca, and he needed some tunes. And I was always pretty good at making little tunes, you know, to sound like Dixley and tunes. So I'd write a sketch and send it up to him that recorded. I'd write the trumpet part, the piano part, the bass part, you know, just small things like that, little outlines. And these are the things he recorded. What were the tunes you wrote?
What was the name of the album? That's a good question. Obviously you didn't go out and buy many jazz records. You didn't buy your own.

I had them, but these were the old shellac records and some of them busted. One of them was Mr. Brown Goes to Town. Model after the picture, Mr. Deeds Goes to Washington. I had another called Swing In, Swing Out, when the word swing was very popular. I think that's the one that did about the best. I got royalties of about 12 cents from some sales in Africa, even. I was very proud of that. These were not ones you played on. Beg your pardon?
You didn't play on these yourself. You just worked on them.

No, no, no. Schalke had his own band up there. As a matter of fact, Barry Pollock recorded a couple of those things with him and he had some fine guys. I don't think he had too many local guys. I think Frankie Federico might have made a couple with him, of course Frankie was up there then with Louie, but he had really all guys from let's say the New York

area. He wouldn't use Bill Bourgeois. Isn't that funny? I don't know why. Yeah. But you know, it always struck me as strange. I think Bill was a little hurt, you know. He's working with Schalke and Schalke with the New Zealand on the record, maybe. I don't know. Bill played a pretty good player in the two. Well, you recorded with Schalke too, didn't you?

Well, that was done down here. We made a record down here. And one side of that was Yes She Does, No She Don't, and I forget the Everybody Lows My Baby or something like that was on the other side. Yeah, I remember that. We made that in the Roosevelt Hotel. And strangely enough, the guy who founded Decca was the guy who recorded that thing. It was the name Cap. Dave or Jack, one of the two. Yeah, he was in, he was the one that made the session. I remember that.
Trevor Richards has something. See people collecting your records still.
Can I buy them back? Like TV rights, huh?
Yeah. I hate to tell you, but you sound pretty good.

You know, it was a good band. I like tenor. I cut my teeth on alto, but I could never really control an alto. I never felt like I had an alto saxophone under control. It was an instrument of the devil, you know. But tenor, I got along very well with tenor. And I had enough musical background. In fact, at that time when tenor began, the tenor bands became very popular, I had no problem reading the alto parts, which is a transposition. As a matter of fact, I thank God I never had any trouble with any transposition. When I used to play the carnival ball with Tornel Luop, I used to read all the violin parts to reinforce the violin sections. I didn't play with the saxophone section. So you did a lot of transposing? Oh yeah. I didn't have any trouble, you know. It's one of those things that you either have a knack for or you don't. There's no secret to it. There's no great education to it. You have a fast eye and you have a fast ear and you get by. And a fast mind.
Who was in that band with Sharpie, huh? When you recorded? Do you remember any of those?

Yes, I played tenor, I think Meyer Weinberg, Gene Meyer was his professional name, played clarinet, Augie Chalang was on drums, and I think Panera was on piano, and I think Cink Martin was on bass. Now I would either have to be Cink Martin or Louis Macenta because Schalke used them almost interchangeably
in those days. Did you name a trombone? Or did he have one?

Oh, I would have been Julian Lane if I omitted him, yes. When did you first meet Almond Hug? Oh, I don't know. I guess about a hundred years ago. I knew Almond. The first time I really got to know Almond was when I went to work for the Lloyd County Brothers when they had the place out at the lake. The name escapes me for the moment, a very successful club. And Almond was playing piano because of course that was part of his family, they were brother-in-laws, you see. He had married one of the Lloyd County girls. Talking about Steve and Freddie? Stephen. Well, Freddie was playing guitar, but Steve and Joe, or Erasmus, which was his right name, owned the club. They and Jameli, Andrew Jameli.
What was Mouse Pecoraro's real name? You know the drummer?
Mouse? Santo?
Do you know his middle name by any chance? No, I don't.

Something we could look up somehow. I might be able to find him in the dead files downstairs. Dead in the sense that we don't use him anymore. I don't know how he got the nickname, but that was a distinguishing from Santo to Trombone player. Sure, yeah. And when did you meet him? Oh somewhere, I would say about midway in my career, because he was Santo's younger. And he played a few jobs with us, with the dance band part of the Donbusters. We were playing night jobs, parties of clubs and things like that. And the band would be scattered to the four winds, and whoever Pinky could get to play for that night he would use it. So that's how I got to meet little Pecoraro,
Pec. Yeah. And did you know Frank Mutz, piano player? The name doesn't ring any bells, no. When did you join the union?

I became a member, let me think now, I guess it would have been about 19, about 27. I'd have to look that up myself. The union at that time was on Royal Street in the 300 block, roughly about 305, something like that, on the second or third floor. And I heard about a drive they were having for new members in which the initiation fee was lowered to $15. And so a whole raft of us went in, because in those days, you weren't considered a professional musician unless you were in the union. Because all the guys who played in the theater pits were in the union, all the guys who played in the clubs were in the union, even the dance halls were union jobs, you know. And so it was the distinction between being a skilled amateur and a professional. You joined the union. You had come of age. Your teacher

would tell you, I think you're ready for the union. Yeah, well, the prelude was too joint, you know. Yes. We got preludes from somebody, I can't remember who, somebody like Wilbur Dinkle, Adam Bound. My goodness, that's a good name. Yeah. Well, those guys, obviously they took pride in things. Oh, completely. Save those, save those, every fragility. You mentioned Wilbur Dinkle. Let me

get into one of my famous deviations. Wilbur had the job at the Old Dauphine Theater, which was a burlesque house, and Fazola used to play there with him too. I guess you know that somewhere along the line too. No, I don't remember that. Oh, yes. Oh, yes. They had about a six-piece band to play for the strippers on stage in the comics, and Faz was, he played Wilbur Dinkle. In fact, they were, let's say, drinking partners. They liked to go out together at night. And this was before Faz went off. You know, he was still a local boy in that sense that he hadn't joined the Crosby band yet. As I say, Faz was always a good musician. So he was a youngster then. Oh, yes, absolutely. Absolutely. He could have been more than 16, 17, 18 years old or something like that, maybe 20, I don't know. But he played there. And because this would have been, wait a minute, it's coming back, 29, 30, something like that, because I went into the Palace Pit. They had a modified barrel. The Palace was on the corner of Dauphin in Ivorville, the same exact spot, but a block away from the Lyric Theater on Burgundy in Ivorville. They had, for a long time, they had vaudeville. And I played the vaudeville show there for a while. That was long after the heyday for the Palace, when they had famous people on in the pit there. And that thing only lasted about, for me, about six or eight weeks. This would have been roughly, either in the 29 or the late 30, something like that. Did you often play jobs with Bozola? Oh, yes, I played a lot of jobs at Faz. I told you we played at the old Hollywood Dance Hall and I played any number of jobs at Faz. Faz and I were good friends. I mean, really good friends. Yeah.
Is this the third rail? Right.
Okay. We were talking about Fazila, Dave, and you said you played in several groups with him, the Hollywood.

Well yes, I was an organized band at the Hollywood, and of course he played with us on the staff of the Dawn Busters in a lot of parts of his life, but then I had played any number of jobs that let's say disorganized, somebody has a job at night and you play with them. So I knew Faz, let's say, practically all of my mature professional life.
And how many instruments did he play then?
As best I know, Faz only played...

Where are we, on the fourth reel? Okay. I want to watch the time, too, because I don't know what your next phone is. That's all right. Okay. You were talking about the Click. What was the Royal Family? That was the Click. That's the same thing?

That was the name that the guys in the general business had given to us, because we had all the shows. But to give you an idea of why it was the Click and why, we were playing, uh, at the old Civic Theater, we were playing Guys and Dolls when it came down here. And the opening, I think, of the third act is when, uh, the scene is supposed to be in Cuba, if you're pardon the expression, uh, when
What's your name?
I'm David Weinstein.
Is that your full name?
That's the only two I have.
And you're . What's today's date so we'll have it?
Today is the 22nd of September, 1988. And where are we? We're in the Board of Directors meeting room of Local 174-496 of the American Federation of Musicians.
Okay. Well, that's good. When were you born and where?
I was born on the 18th of December, 1909 on Royal Street right in the back of St. Louis Cathedral, right in the heart of the French Quarter.
That's good. Let me look at the questions.
